video_title: What the 2026 Midterm Elections Mean for Crypto Regulation and the Clarity Act
gist: After a Democratic midterm sweep (popular vote +13), Paradigm's Justin Slaughter and Mike Katz argue the Clarity Act is dead in the lame duck and a stricter House Democratic market-structure bill (tougher DeFi rules, ethics provisions, more SEC jurisdiction) is coming, but existing SEC/CFTC rules will likely stand for two years. The main crypto-related oversight target will be Trump family crypto deals (World Liberty, meme coins, the CZ pardon); GENIUS Act implementation is exposed to appropriations riders and bank lobbying, and the industry needs a good-faith reset with Democrats before 2028 rather than relying on Fairshake super PAC money.

themes.theme: Clarity Act dead, Democratic rewrite coming

insights.claim: Justin Slaughter says the Clarity Act crypto market structure bill is effectively dead and will not pass in the lame-duck session; he gave it only 5% odds even before the midterms.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: No US crypto market-structure statute before 2027 at the earliest; legal-status discount on tokens and DeFi persists.
insights.quote: So, to break some news, clarity does look dead. I don't think it passes in the lame duck. I gave it 5% odds before the election.

insights.claim: House Financial Services Democratic staff are reportedly drafting their own crypto market structure bill with four likely pillars: stricter ethics rules on officials' crypto holdings, much stricter DeFi rules than the BRCA, Maxine Waters-style consumer protections like 24-hour withdrawal payouts and independent audits, and a shift of more jurisdiction from the CFTC to the SEC.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Any future bill is likely worse for DeFi and for CFTC-favored token classifications than Clarity; DeFi protocols face the biggest regulatory tail risk.

insights.claim: Democrats who follow crypto closely concede roughly 80% of the Clarity Act is acceptable, but the contested 20% includes the provisions the industry cares most about, especially DeFi.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Compromise is possible but will be paid for in DeFi treatment; DeFi tokens carry asymmetric regulatory risk.
insights.quote: they admit, you know, 80% of clarity is fine. We're fighting over 20%. The problem for the industry is part of that 20% are what they really care about.

insights.claim: Maxine Waters' expanded crypto investor and consumer bill of rights would include 24-hour withdrawal rights and mandatory audits, and most importantly a separation of custody and exchange functions in terms of ownership, which is a sticking point for some integrated entities.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Vertically integrated exchange-custodians could face forced structural separation under a Democratic bill, raising compliance costs.

insights.claim: Maxine Waters is the presumptive House Financial Services chair but could be challenged by Sean Casten, who is also antagonistic to crypto.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Committee leadership either way is crypto-skeptical, so House legislation will tilt restrictive.

insights.claim: Crypto policy history over six years is a pattern of near-deals abandoned and regretted: Warren rejected the DCCPA as too weak, then by 2025 released market-structure principles that were essentially the DCCPA, and Democrats may similarly overestimate what they can get in 2029.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Expect continued legislative misses; base case is prolonged regulation-by-agency rather than statute.
insights.quote: The story of crypto policym over the last 6 years has been every time someone has an almost deal and walks away, they regret it.

insights.claim: The industry failed to get Clarity passed because it did not make compromises while Republicans held unified control of government, and now faces more regulation than it would have preferred.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: The window of maximal regulatory favorability has closed; price in a less friendly legislative outcome.

insights.claim: Justin Slaughter expects SEC and CFTC crypto rules to remain unchanged over the next two years, with SEC chair Atkins and CFTC chair Selig continuing their current agendas despite the Democratic Congress.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Agency-driven regulatory relief (exemptive relief, no-action letters, rules) remains the operative regime through 2028.
insights.quote: The short answer is I don't think the rules change over the next two years.

insights.claim: Atkins reportedly understands he should avoid the past-chair mistake of pushing 30 to 40 rules and instead finalize a few rules, while facing many oversight hearings that the Trump administration is happy to engage in.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Fewer but more durable SEC crypto rules; narrower scope of relief than some hope.

insights.claim: A small but real risk is that Democrats attach an appropriations rider that halts specific crypto rulemakings, including GENIUS Act implementing rules.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Watch appropriations bills as the concrete mechanism by which a Democratic Congress could stall crypto rules.

insights.claim: Mike Katz argues the industry should accept that it won't get everything and push for sticky rules designed to survive court challenges and a future hostile Democratic administration replacing agency heads.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Durability of current agency rules, not breadth, determines long-run value for regulated crypto businesses.

insights.claim: Midterm results pose a live risk that the administration trims its sails on AI and data center policy, unlike crypto where Slaughter expects no change.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Political risk is shifting toward AI infrastructure rather than crypto agency policy.

insights.claim: The GENIUS Act stablecoin law takes effect January 17, 2027 regardless of whether rules are final, but only the OCC has finalized its rule while several other agencies have not.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Stablecoin issuers face an effective date with incomplete rulemaking, creating implementation uncertainty and openings for opponents.

insights.claim: Mike Katz argues banks are doing everything in their power to sabotage the GENIUS Act and will use the new Democratic Congress, which controls agency funding and oversight, to make implementation hard even though the statute cannot be unwritten.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Stablecoin growth thesis faces implementation drag from bank lobbying via appropriations and oversight levers.
insights.quote: The new Congress can't unwrite the statute, but they can make life hard for the people implementing it.

insights.claim: Mike Katz says waiting out the Democratic Congress until 2028 would be a gigantic mistake because Democrats, banks, and other players will not wait.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Firms that engage proactively with Democrats may gain regulatory advantage over those that disengage.
insights.quote: That that in my opinion would be a gigantic mistake. I don't think the Democrats are going to wait. I don't think the banks are going to wait.

insights.claim: Crypto-related congressional oversight will prioritize Trump family crypto dealings, including meme coins and World Liberty funding linked to the UAE and Saudi Arabia, looking for self-dealing, quid pro quo, and foreign influence using new subpoena power.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Headline and subpoena risk concentrates on World Liberty and counterparties tied to Trump crypto ventures.

insights.claim: Because the oversight spotlight will be on Trump family crypto businesses, other crypto companies have an opening to work with the broader Democratic majority on productive solutions.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Crypto firms distanced from Trump ventures may be relatively insulated and better positioned politically.

insights.claim: Maxine Waters tied the Binance hack, within 24 hours, to Trump's pardon of CZ and the dropped cases, and Democrats will investigate whether political donations were exchanged for pardons or dismissed cases, though they cannot unring the SEC's enforcement shift.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Binance faces renewed congressional scrutiny, but reversal of dismissed SEC cases is unlikely.

insights.claim: Justin Slaughter says Gensler-era SEC crypto cases were weak and likely to lose at the Supreme Court, which would have produced a ruling that crypto is unregulated, but many Democrats never accepted this.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Dismissed enforcement cases are unlikely to be revived; the legal floor favored the industry anyway.

insights.claim: Because executive privilege limits direct oversight of administrations, Democrats' most effective tool will be subpoenaing corporations for their communications with the administration.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Crypto companies that dealt with the Trump administration face document-request and subpoena exposure.

insights.claim: A reported 181-page dossier lists executives and companies as targets of a new Democratic oversight effort spanning prediction markets, sports, Wall Street, meatpacking, AI and crypto, which Senator Warren reportedly views with approval; Slaughter expects intense letters and hearings but limited results.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Expect headline risk for prediction markets and crypto executives, but low probability of substantive policy change.

insights.claim: Democrats won the 2026 midterm popular vote by 13 points versus 8 in the 2006 wave, flipping states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, which Slaughter calls the end of the long 2016 rather than a permanent new norm.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: The swing is unlikely to repeat at this scale in 2028, so policy hostility should not be extrapolated linearly.
insights.quote: this was a year where the Democrats won the popular vote by 13 points. As a point of comparison, in 2006, which is the last great Democratic midterm wave, they won it by eight.

insights.claim: Many new millennial Democratic members have owned crypto or know someone who does, and senator-elect James Talarico voted for a Bitcoin state fund in the Texas Senate, so freshmen are not reflexively anti-crypto.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: The Democratic caucus is more crypto-neutral than its leadership; a moderate bloc could block extreme measures.

insights.claim: Slaughter's contrarian take: Sherrod Brown won only a two-year Senate term by about four points despite a D+13 year, so he will focus on 2028 re-election from the Agriculture Committee rather than on crypto, though he will not help crypto.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: The Ag committee, which oversees digital assets and prediction markets, may be less hostile than feared.

insights.claim: Freshmen on Senate Banking consistently leave it quickly because it is so contentious, so Warren's fierce oversight agenda may clash with junior members who do not want a holy war against corporate America ahead of 2028.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Warren's chairmanship power is constrained by her rank-and-file, limiting legislative hostility.

insights.claim: Elizabeth Warren is not anti-bank per se but opposes large banks while favoring small banks, a nuance the crypto industry misread.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Crypto pitches framed as helping community and regional banks may find more traction than anti-bank framing.

insights.claim: A faction of roughly 30 to 40 Democratic staffers wants to vindicate the Biden administration and get revenge, viewing Trump as a symptom of corporate power, but Slaughter expects this to produce painful hearings rather than much more.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Oversight noise likely exceeds actual policy impact on crypto.

insights.claim: Slaughter warns that if the industry does not rebuild bridges with Democrats over the next two years, a strong Democratic 2028 could be very dangerous for crypto, potentially worse than the Biden era.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: 2028 is the key long-horizon regulatory tail risk for crypto valuations.

insights.claim: Fairshake spent $56 million trying to defeat Sherrod Brown and he still won, while total Texas spending of around $500 million also failed to stop the wave, showing money could not overcome the midterm swing.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Crypto's political war chest has lost its intimidation value; legislative leverage is weaker than assumed.
insights.quote: You cannot think of super PAC spending as your first weapon. It is your last weapon of last resort.

insights.claim: Mike Katz argues the post-2024 assumption that crypto's war chest would intimidate Democrats into backing industry legislation is now broken and the fear factor is gone.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Industry must win on merits; expect slower, more compromise-heavy policy outcomes.
insights.quote: the lessons of this election are, you know, that the fear factor is gone.

insights.claim: In the late Clarity negotiations, the 12 Democrats were not seeking a fig leaf but needed merits-based justification, and emphasizing the industry's money cannon likely hurt rather than helped.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Future deals depend on substantive concessions, not lobbying spend.
insights.quote: Saying we have this big money cannon is not going to actually get you over the line.

insights.claim: Mike Katz says extreme crypto-industry partisans mirror Elizabeth Warren's extremism, a horseshoe dynamic, and the industry should openly criticize Trump family crypto enrichment while supporting sensible market structure.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Industry repositioning away from Trump-aligned politics is a precondition for bipartisan legislation.
insights.quote: the extremism of of some members of the crypto industry honestly mirrors their antagonist in Elizabeth Warren and her extremism. It's just like it's the horseshoe theory.

insights.claim: Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa wants to halt new data center approvals pending rules on electricity and water costs, but Slaughter expects existing and under-construction projects to finish, making it more a problem for hyperscalers than Bitcoin miners.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Existing Texas miner/AI hosting capacity gains scarcity value while new Texas data center pipelines face delay.

insights.claim: Slaughter would advise AI data center builders that they are too centralized in America and should build abroad, since other countries want the capacity for influence, though the Trump administration prefers domestic builds; he expects more AI data center buildout abroad.
insights.speaker: Justin Slaughter
insights.so_what: Non-US data center developers and sites may benefit from US political friction over power and water.

insights.claim: Mike Katz notes the Texas governor-elect is proposing limits rather than a total data center ban, and Greg Abbott himself moderated on data centers as political winds shifted.
insights.speaker: Mike Katz
insights.so_what: Data center backlash is bipartisan; expect permitting conditions rather than outright bans.
